## 6. Periodic descent

Fix $d \mid n$ and let $\pi : \mathbb{Z}/n \to \mathbb{Z}/d$ be the canonical ring homomorphism.

**Definition 6.1.** The *pullback* $\mathrm{pull} : \mathrm{Config}(d) \to \mathrm{Config}(n)$ is $(\mathrm{pull}\, t)(i) = t(\pi(i))$. Its image consists exactly of the $d$-periodic configurations.

**Theorem 6.2 (Simulation embedding).** For every local rule $g$ and every $d \mid n$, the map $\mathrm{pull}$ is injective and intertwines the dynamics:
$$F_g(\mathrm{pull}\, t) = \mathrm{pull}(F_g\, t).$$
Consequently $\mathrm{pull}$ is a morphism of dynamical systems: $t \in V(g,d) \iff \mathrm{pull}\, t \in V(g,n)$, and by Lemma 5.6,
$$\mathrm{per}(F_g, \mathrm{pull}\, t) = \mathrm{per}(F_g, t).$$

*Proof sketch.* $\pi$ is a ring homomorphism, so $\pi(i \pm 1) = \pi(i) \pm 1$; the local rule therefore sees exactly the same neighbourhood after pullback. Injectivity holds because $\pi$ is surjective. $\square$

**Corollary 6.3 (Divisibility monotonicity).** For every rule $g$ and every $d \mid n$, $\#V(g,d) \le \#V(g,n)$. Likewise every exact orbit length occurring at size $d$ occurs at size $n$.

**Lemma 6.4 (Descent).** Suppose $s \in \mathrm{Config}(n)$ satisfies $s(i + d) = s(i)$ for all $i$, where $d \mid n$. Then $s = \mathrm{pull}\, t$ for some $t \in \mathrm{Config}(d)$.

*Proof sketch.* Set $t(x) = s(\bar{x})$ where $\bar x \in \{0,\dots,d-1\}$ is the canonical representative. Writing $\mathrm{val}(i) = (\mathrm{val}(i) \bmod d) + d\lfloor \mathrm{val}(i)/d \rfloor$ and iterating the $d$-periodicity hypothesis $\lfloor \mathrm{val}(i)/d\rfloor$ times gives $s(i) = t(\pi(i))$. $\square$

**Theorem 6.5 (Count invariance under descent).** Let $d \mid n$ and suppose every $s \in V(g,n)$ is $d$-periodic. Then
$$\#V(g,n) = \#V(g,d).$$

*Proof sketch.* By Lemma 6.4 and Theorem 6.2, $V(g,n) = \mathrm{pull}(V(g,d))$; apply injectivity. $\square$

**Lemma 6.6 (Coprime collapse).** If $d$ is invertible modulo $n$ — equivalently $\gcd(d,n) = 1$ — then any $d$-periodic $s \in \mathrm{Config}(n)$ is constant.

*Proof sketch.* If $d v = 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}/n$, then for any $i,j$ set $u = v(j-i)$, so $d u = j - i$. Iterating $d$-periodicity $\mathrm{val}(u)$ times from $i$ gives $s(i + du) = s(i)$, i.e. $s(j) = s(i)$. $\square$

Theorem 6.5 and Lemma 6.6 together cover all $n$ once the "period" $d$ of a rule's fixed-point equation is known: sizes divisible by $d$ reduce to the single finite computation at size $d$, and sizes coprime to $d$ collapse to constants. For $d$ prime, as in all our applications, these two cases are exhaustive.

## 7. Exact counting functions

### 7.1 Rule 150

**Lemma 7.1.** $s \in V(150,n)$ if and only if $s(i-1) = s(i+1)$ for all $i$, i.e. if and only if $s$ is $2$-periodic. Every constant configuration is fixed.

*Proof.* The fixed-point equation is $s(i-1) + s(i) + s(i+1) = s(i)$, i.e. $s(i-1) + s(i+1) = 0$, i.e. $s(i-1) = s(i+1)$. Constants satisfy $c+c+c = c$ since $2c = 0$. $\square$

**Theorem 7.2.** For every $n \ge 1$,
$$\#V(150,n) = \begin{cases} 4, & 2 \mid n,\\ 2, & 2 \nmid n.\end{cases}$$

*Proof sketch.* If $n$ is even, Theorem 6.5 with $d = 2$ gives $\#V(150,n) = \#V(150,2)$, and direct inspection of the four configurations of length $2$ shows all are fixed: $\#V(150,2) = 4$. If $n$ is odd, $2$ is invertible mod $n$, so by Lemma 6.6 every fixed configuration is constant; both constants are fixed and they are distinct, giving $2$. $\square$

### 7.2 Rule 90

**Lemma 7.3 ($3$-periodicity).** Every $s \in V(90,n)$ satisfies $s(i+3) = s(i)$.

*Proof sketch.* The fixed-point equation is the $\mathbb{F}_2$ Fibonacci recurrence $s(i-1) + s(i+1) = s(i)$, equivalently $s(i+1) = s(i) + s(i-1)$. Applying it at $i+1$ and $i+2$ and adding, the middle terms cancel because $2 = 0$, leaving $s(i+3) = s(i)$. (Equivalently: the Fibonacci recurrence over $\mathbb{F}_2$ has Pisano period $3$.) $\square$

**Theorem 7.4.** For every $n \ge 1$,
$$\#V(90,n) = \begin{cases} 4, & 3 \mid n,\\ 1, & 3 \nmid n.\end{cases}$$

*Proof sketch.* If $3 \mid n$, Theorem 6.5 with $d = 3$ reduces to $\#V(90,3) = 4$, a check over $8$ configurations. If $3 \nmid n$, then $3$ is invertible mod $n$, so by Lemmas 7.3 and 6.6 every fixed configuration is constant; the equation at a constant $c$ reads $c + c = c$, i.e. $c = 0$. Hence $V(90,n) = \{0\}$. $\square$

### 7.3 Rule 30

Rule $30$ is nonlinear, so no recurrence argument applies directly; nevertheless the same descent machinery works after a case analysis.

**Lemma 7.5 (Cleared fixed-point relation).** $s \in V(30,n)$ if and only if for all $i$,
$$s(i-1) + s(i+1) + s(i)\,s(i+1) = 0 .$$

*Proof.* The equation $s(i-1) + s(i) + s(i+1) + s(i)s(i+1) = s(i)$ simplifies by cancelling $s(i)$. $\square$

**Lemma 7.6 ($2$-periodicity).** Every $s \in V(30,n)$ satisfies $s(i+2) = s(i)$.

*Proof sketch.* Apply Lemma 7.5 at $i+1$: $s(i) + s(i+2) + s(i+1)s(i+2) = 0$. If $s(i+1) = 0$ this reads $s(i) = s(i+2)$ directly. If $s(i+1) = 1$ it gives $s(i) = 0$; applying the relation at $i+2$ then shows $s(i+2) = 1$ is impossible (it would force $1 = 0$), so $s(i+2) = 0 = s(i)$. $\square$

**Theorem 7.7.** For every $n \ge 1$,
$$\#V(30,n) = \begin{cases} 3, & 2 \mid n,\\ 1, & 2 \nmid n.\end{cases}$$

*Proof sketch.* For even $n$, descend to $d = 2$: the fixed configurations of length $2$ are $00$, $01$, $10$, giving $3$ (the configuration $11$ fails). For odd $n$, $2$ is invertible, so every fixed configuration is constant by Lemmas 7.6 and 6.6; a constant $c$ must satisfy $c + c + c^2 = 0$, i.e. $c^2 = 0$ since $2c = 0$, hence $c = 0$. $\square$

**Remark 7.8.** Rule $30$ is the standard chaotic exemplar, yet its fixed-point count is as tame and as periodic in $n$ as those of the additive rules. What the counts record is the period of the recurrence cutting out the fixed set — $2$, $3$, $2$ for rules $150$, $90$, $30$ — an invariant of the *linearisation* of the rule, not of its dynamical complexity.

### 7.4 A count equal to two: the traffic rule

**Lemma 7.9 (Leftward transitivity of the lattice).** Let $P$ be a property of sites such that $P(i) \Rightarrow P(i-1)$ for all $i$, and suppose $P(i_0)$ holds for some $i_0$. Then $P$ holds at every site.

*Proof sketch.* Induction gives $P(i_0 - k)$ for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$; every site is of that form by the mirror of Lemma 3.5. $\square$

**Definition 7.10 (Constant-pair criterion).** A local rule $g$ satisfies the *constant-pair criterion* if
1. *(zeros travel left)* $g(a,0,c) = 0 \Rightarrow a = 0$;
2. *(ones travel right)* $g(a,1,c) = 1 \Rightarrow c = 1$;
3. $g(0,0,0) = 0$ and $g(1,1,1) = 1$.

**Theorem 7.11 (Constant-Pair Theorem).** If $g$ satisfies the constant-pair criterion then for every $n \ge 1$
$$V(g,n) = \{\, \mathbf{0},\ \mathbf{1} \,\}, \qquad \#V(g,n) = 2,$$
where $\mathbf{0}$ and $\mathbf{1}$ are the two constant configurations.

*Proof sketch.* Let $s$ be fixed. If some coordinate vanishes, say $s(i) = 0$, then fixedness at $i$ gives $g(s(i-1), 0, s(i+1)) = 0$, so by condition 1, $s(i-1) = 0$; Lemma 7.9 propagates this around the lattice and $s = \mathbf{0}$. If no coordinate vanishes then $s = \mathbf{1}$. Conversely conditions 3 make both constants fixed, and they are distinct. $\square$

**Corollary 7.12 (Census).** Exactly four elementary rules satisfy the constant-pair criterion, namely $176$, $178$, $184$ and $186$. In particular the traffic rule $184$ has exactly two fixed configurations on every cyclic lattice, and so does its mirror image (by Corollary 5.4).

**Remark 7.13.** Condition 2 of the criterion is not used in the proof of $V \subseteq \{\mathbf 0, \mathbf 1\}$; it is retained because it is the natural dual of condition 1, it is the transparent statement of the traffic interpretation ("cars advance into empty space ahead"), and it is what makes the criterion invariant in spirit under the mirror symmetry. Under the traffic reading of Rule $184$ — $1$ for an occupied cell, $0$ for empty road, a car advancing exactly when the cell ahead is free — the theorem says that on a ring road the only stationary traffic states are the empty road and the complete jam, at every ring size.

**Remark 7.14 (Sufficiency, not necessity).** Both propagation criteria are sufficient conditions only. There exist rules with $\#V \equiv 2$ that fail the constant-pair criterion (for instance rules whose two fixed configurations form a nonconstant shift orbit), and enumeration shows exactly $78$ rules have $\#V(g,n) = 1$ for all $n \le 7$, of which only $48$ are certified for all $n$ by Theorem 5.8. Closing the remaining gap is Conjecture 10.1.

---

## 8. Orbits: what fixed points miss

**Theorem 8.1 (Universal existence of periodic orbits).** For every local rule $g$ and every $n \ge 1$ there exist $s \in \mathrm{Config}(n)$ and $k > 0$ with $F_g^{\,k}(s) = s$.

*Proof sketch.* The orbit $k \mapsto F_g^{\,k}(0)$ takes values in a finite set, so $F_g^{\,a}(0) = F_g^{\,b}(0)$ for some $a < b$; then $F_g^{\,a}(0)$ is periodic with period $b - a > 0$. $\square$

**Theorem 8.2 (Rule 51).** Rule $51$, $g(a,b,c) = 1+b$, is an involution on $\mathrm{Config}(n)$ with no fixed configuration whatsoever: $\#V(51,n) = 0$ for every $n \ge 1$. Every configuration has exact period exactly $2$.

*Proof sketch.* $F_{51}$ is pointwise complementation, hence involutive since $2 = 0$. It fixes no configuration since $1 + s(0) = s(0)$ is impossible. Hence the exact period divides $2$ and is not $1$. $\square$

**Theorem 8.3 (Rule 170: unbounded orbit lengths).** Let $\delta$ be the configuration with $\delta(0) = 1$ and $\delta(i) = 0$ otherwise. Under Rule $170$ (the left shift), $\delta$ is $k$-periodic if and only if $n \mid k$; its exact period is therefore $n$.

*Proof sketch.* By Proposition 3.2 and Corollary 3.4, $F_{170}^{\,k} s = s(\cdot + k)$. Evaluating at $0$, $F_{170}^{\,k}\delta = \delta$ forces $\delta(k) = 1$, i.e. $k = 0$ in $\mathbb{Z}/n$. Conversely $n \mid k$ makes the translation trivial. $\square$

So the fixed-point count of Rule $170$ is the constant $2$ (its fixed configurations are exactly the constants) while its exact orbit lengths grow linearly in $n$: the fixed-point statistic is genuinely lossy.

**Theorem 8.4 (An exact two-cycle of Rule 110).** Let $t = 1110 \in \mathrm{Config}(4)$. Then $F_{110}^{\,2}(t) = t$ and $F_{110}(t) \ne t$, so $\mathrm{per}(F_{110}, t) = 2$. Consequently, by Theorem 6.2, for every $n$ with $4 \mid n$ there is a configuration $s \in \mathrm{Config}(n)$ with $\mathrm{per}(F_{110}, s) = 2$, and $s \ne 0$.

*Proof sketch.* The two finite facts about $t$ are direct computations on the $4$-site lattice. Transport to size $n$ is by the simulation embedding, which preserves exact periods. That $s \ne 0$ follows since $0$ is the unique fixed configuration and has exact period $1 \ne 2$. $\square$

Explicitly, on $\mathrm{Config}(4)$ the configurations satisfying $F_{110}^{\,2}(s) = s$ are $0000$, $1110$, $1011$, $1101$, $0111$, forming the fixed point together with two $2$-cycles $1110 \leftrightarrow 1011$ and $1101 \leftrightarrow 0111$. These are the smallest glider-like objects of Rule $110$, and their existence at *every* size divisible by $4$ is the content of Theorem 8.4.

**Theorem 8.5 (Separation results).** For every $n \ge 1$:
1. $\#V(90,n) \ne \#V(110,n)$ if and only if $3 \mid n$;
2. $\#V(110,n) < \#V(150,n)$ always;
3. $\#V(184,n) = 2 \ne 1 = \#V(110,n)$ always;
4. $\#V(46,n) = \#V(110,n)$ always, and likewise for the other $15$ rules of the census of Corollary 4.6 and for the three symmetry partners $124, 137, 193$.

Items 1–3 show the statistic is not useless; item 4 shows precisely what it cannot do. Universality is invisible to it.

---

## 9. The polynomial and scheme-theoretic model

The counting results above can be recast as statements about rational points of affine schemes over $\mathbb{F}_2$, which is the natural home for uniform-in-$n$ statements.

**Definition 9.1 (Rule polynomials).** For a local rule $g$ and a site $i \in \mathbb{Z}/n$ define
$$P_{g,i} \;=\; \sum_{a,b,c \in \mathbb{F}_2} g(a,b,c)\,\big(1 + a + X_{i-1}\big)\big(1 + b + X_i\big)\big(1 + c + X_{i+1}\big) \;\in\; \mathbb{F}_2[X_j : j \in \mathbb{Z}/n].$$
The factor $1 + a + X_j$ is the $\mathbb{F}_2$ indicator of the event $X_j = a$.

**Theorem 9.2 (Evaluation is the update map).** For every configuration $s$ and site $i$,
$$P_{g,i}(s) = (F_g s)(i).$$

*Proof sketch.* Expanding, the identity reduces to the finite statement
$$\sum_{a,b,c} g(a,b,c)(1+a+x)(1+b+y)(1+c+z) = g(x,y,z)$$
for all $x,y,z \in \mathbb{F}_2$, which holds because $(1+a+x)$ equals $1$ when $x = a$ and $0$ otherwise, so exactly one summand survives. $\square$

**Theorem 9.3 (Polynomial shift equivariance).** Renaming the variables by $X_j \mapsto X_{j+i}$ carries $P_{g,0}$ to $P_{g,i}$.

**Definition 9.4 (Fixed-point ideal).** Let
$$I(g,n) = \big( \{P_{g,i} - X_i\}_{i \in \mathbb{Z}/n} \;\cup\; \{X_i^2 - X_i\}_{i \in \mathbb{Z}/n} \big) \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2[X_j : j \in \mathbb{Z}/n].$$
The second family is the Boolean relation set, forcing the coordinates to be bits.

**Theorem 9.5 (Rational points).** A configuration $s$ satisfies $P(s) = 0$ for every $P \in I(g,n)$ if and only if $s \in V(g,n)$. That is, the $\mathbb{F}_2$-points of the fixed-point ideal are exactly the fixed configurations.

*Proof sketch.* Forwards: apply the hypothesis to the generator $P_{g,i} - X_i$ and use Theorem 9.2 to get $(F_g s)(i) = s(i)$. Backwards: each generator lies in the kernel of evaluation at $s$ — the update generators by Theorem 9.2, the Boolean generators because $c^2 = c$ for $c \in \mathbb{F}_2$ — and the kernel is an ideal, so it contains the span. $\square$

**Corollary 9.6.** $I(110,n) \ne (1)$ for every $n \ge 1$: the coordinate ring of the fixed-point scheme of Rule $110$ is nonzero, since $0 \in V(110,n)$ is a rational point.

In this language, Theorems 7.2, 7.4, 7.7 compute the number of $\mathbb{F}_2$-rational points of an explicit family of affine schemes whose defining equations depend on $n$ only through the cyclic index group, and the periodicity of the point-counts in $n$ is the arithmetic shadow of that dependence.

---

## 10. Algorithms

Three algorithms underlie the computational side of this work.

**A. Transfer-matrix point count.** The fixed configurations of $g$ on $\mathbb{Z}/n$ are exactly the closed walks of length $n$ in the *fixed de Bruijn graph* $D(g)$: vertices are the four overlapping pairs $(a,b) \in \mathbb{F}_2^2$, and there is an edge $(a,b) \to (b,c)$ precisely when $g(a,b,c) = b$. Writing $M(g)$ for its $4\times 4$ adjacency matrix,
$$\#V(g,n) = \operatorname{tr} M(g)^n .$$
This computes any single count in $O(\log n)$ matrix multiplications of fixed size $4$, versus $\Theta(n 2^n)$ for brute-force enumeration, and it explains structurally every phenomenon above: a constant count $1$ corresponds to a graph with exactly one cycle, and a count periodic in $n$ with period $p$ corresponds to a spectrum of roots of unity of order dividing $p$ together with nilpotent directions.

**B. Descent certification.** To prove a formula for $\#V(g,\cdot)$ valid for all $n$: (1) find the smallest $d$ such that every fixed configuration is $d$-periodic — over $\mathbb{F}_2$ this is the period of the recurrence, detectable from $M(g)$; (2) compute $\#V(g,d)$ by enumeration of $2^d$ configurations; (3) for $n$ with $d \mid n$, conclude $\#V(g,n) = \#V(g,d)$; (4) for $n$ coprime to $d$, solve the constant case by hand. For prime $d$ the two cases are exhaustive.

**C. Symmetry-closed census.** For each of the $256$ rule numbers, test the local singleton criterion on the rule and on its three symmetry partners; accept if any passes. The test inspects four truth-table entries per rule, so the census costs $O(256 \cdot 4 \cdot 4)$ elementary operations. It certifies $48$ rules.

---

## 11. Discussion

The results assemble into a single methodological point. There are three genuinely different reasons why $\#V(g,n)$ can be determined for all $n$ at once:

* a **local** reason (an entry of the truth table forces a bit to propagate, and cyclicity closes the argument);
* a **conjugacy** reason (the rule is a coordinate change away from one already understood);
* an **arithmetic** reason (the fixed-point equations are a recurrence of period $d$, and divisibility of $n$ by $d$ decides the count).

Fifty-two of the $256$ rules are covered by the first two mechanisms alone; the third handles the additive rules $90$ and $150$ and, more interestingly, the nonlinear Rule $30$.

Against this, the negative results are sharp. The count is a class function for a group of order four; it depends on Rule $110$ only through four bits of its table, which it shares with fifteen other rules including a rule of a different qualitative class; and it is constant in $n$ for the shift rule $170$, whose orbit lengths grow linearly. Any claim of a correlation between fixed-point statistics and a qualitative classification of automata must therefore specify at minimum: the boundary convention, the range of sizes, the exact statistic, and the classification data — and must survive the fact that no such statistic distinguishes Rule $46$ from Rule $110$ at any size.

The constructive alternative is the orbit spectrum. It is finer (it distinguishes Rules $51$ and $110$, which the fixed-point count also distinguishes, but also Rules $170$ and $240$ from constant-count rules at large $n$), it is still a class function for the symmetry group, and it transports along divisibility of lattice sizes by an *injective simulation embedding*. Since universality is a statement about unbounded space-time evolution, embeddings and orbit structures are the right invariants to pursue.

---

## 12. Future directions

The following conjectures are the sharpest questions the results raise; each is falsifiable by a finite computation or a single counterexample.

**Conjecture 12.1 (Finite certification of the singleton property).** For an elementary rule $g$ the following are equivalent: (i) $\#V(g,n) = 1$ for every $n \ge 1$; (ii) $\#V(g,n) = 1$ for $n = 1,\dots,7$; (iii) the only bi-infinite $g$-fixed word is the all-zero word. Enumeration shows that the set of rules satisfying (ii) has exactly $78$ elements; $48$ of them are certified by the symmetry-closed criterion, so the conjecture predicts exactly $30$ further rules whose unit count needs a non-local argument. The key insight is that $\#V(g,n) = \operatorname{tr} M(g)^n$ for the $4 \times 4$ fixed de Bruijn matrix of §10, so a count that stays $1$ forever means that graph has a unique cycle — a decidable property of a four-vertex graph. Hence a finite test must exist; the only question is how small it can be.

**Further programme.**

1. Derive additional named singleton theorems as concrete corollaries of the right-transitivity criterion, with periodic left and right shifts as explicit primitives.
2. Replace Boolean algebraic normal forms by polynomials over $\mathbb{F}_2$ throughout and prove equality of polynomial evaluation with the global update map in that setting.
3. Specify the fixed-point coordinate ring using both the update equations and the Boolean relations $x_i^2 - x_i$; study its Krull dimension separately from its number of $\mathbb{F}_2$-rational points.
4. Formalise all $256$ rule tables from rule numbers and prove that rule-number decoding is a bijection with the set of local rules.
5. Compute fixed-point counts for every rule and bounded lattice size, then compare those finite invariants with a precisely encoded qualitative classification. Any correlation claim should state the boundary convention, size range, statistic, and classification data explicitly.
6. Study periodic orbits of length greater than one. Universality concerns unbounded space-time evolution, so orbit structure and simulation embeddings are more relevant invariants than fixed points alone.
7. Formulate any sheaf-theoretic construction explicitly: give the site, topology, restriction maps, and the intended theorem relating global sections to configurations, before comparing section structure across rules.

\begin{abstract}
We study the fixed-point sets of elementary cellular automata on cyclic lattices, uniformly in the lattice size. Writing $V(g,n)$ for the set of configurations $s : \mathbb{Z}/n \to \FF$ satisfying $s_i = g(s_{i-1}, s_i, s_{i+1})$ for all $i$, we obtain complete descriptions of $V(g,n)$ for large families of the $256$ elementary rules, valid for every $n \ge 1$ simultaneously.
Four kinds of result are proved. \emph{(i) Propagation criteria.} A rule satisfying the three local conditions ``$g(a,0,c)=0 \Rightarrow c=0$'', ``$g(1,1,1)\ne 1$'' and ``$g(0,0,0)=0$'' has $V(g,n)=\{0\}$ for every $n$; these conditions are equivalent to fixing four bits of the rule number, so exactly $16$ rules are certified, Rule $110$ among them. A companion two-sided criterion (``zeros travel left, ones travel right'') forces $V(g,n)$ to be exactly the two constant configurations; exactly $4$ rules satisfy it, namely $176$, $178$, $184$, $186$, including the traffic rule $184$. \emph{(ii) Symmetry.} Reflection and complementation are realised as conjugacies of the global dynamics, so the fixed-point count and the entire exact-period spectrum are class functions for the resulting Klein four-group; closing the singleton census under the group yields $48$ certified rules, and Rules $124$, $137$, $193$ inherit the Rule $110$ singleton theorem. \emph{(iii) Periodic descent.} For $d \mid n$ the pullback along $\mathbb{Z}/n \twoheadrightarrow \mathbb{Z}/d$ is an injective simulation embedding of dynamical systems, yielding monotonicity, exact count invariance under $d$-periodicity, and preservation of exact orbit periods; combined with a coprimality collapse this gives $\#V(150,n) = 4$ or $2$ according as $n$ is even or odd, $\#V(90,n)=4$ or $1$ according as $3 \mid n$ or not, and $\#V(30,n)=3$ or $1$ according as $n$ is even or odd. \emph{(iv) Scheme-theoretic model.} Explicit interpolation polynomials realise the global update map, and the fixed configurations are exactly the $\FF$-points of the ideal generated by the update equations together with the Boolean relations $x_i^2 - x_i$.
We conclude with a negative result: the fixed-point statistic cannot detect computational universality, since Rules $46$ and $110$ agree in all four bits governing the count and hence have identical fixed-point cardinality at every size, whereas orbit-spectrum data is strictly finer.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} elementary cellular automata, Rule 110, fixed-point variety, de Bruijn graph, periodic descent, Klein four-group symmetry, traffic rule 184, $\FF$ polynomial dynamics.

\section{Introduction}

An elementary cellular automaton is specified by a \emph{local rule} $g : \FF^3 \to \FF$. On the cyclic lattice of $n$ sites it induces a \emph{global update map}
\[
F_g : \FF^{\mathbb{Z}/n} \to \FF^{\mathbb{Z}/n}, \qquad (F_g s)(i) = g\big(s(i-1),\, s(i),\, s(i+1)\big).
\]
There are $2^8 = 256$ local rules, indexed by the number whose binary expansion lists the eight outputs. Despite the triviality of the specification, the family contains a computationally universal member (Rule $110$), a standard chaotic exemplar (Rule $30$), the additive rules $90$ and $150$, and the traffic rule $184$.

The object of this paper is the set of \emph{fixed configurations}
\[
V(g,n) := \{ s \in \FF^{\mathbb{Z}/n} : F_g s = s \},
\]
which we call the \emph{fixed-point variety} of $g$ at size $n$, for reasons made precise in Section~\ref{sec:poly}: it is the set of $\FF$-rational points of an explicit affine scheme. Our aim is to determine $\#V(g,\cdot)$ \emph{as a function of $n$}, and to identify the mechanisms that make uniform determinations possible. Three emerge, and they are logically independent: \emph{local propagation amplified by cyclicity}; \emph{conjugacy}, whereby reflection and complementation are changes of coordinates for the dynamics; and \emph{descent along divisibility} of lattice sizes. We also record what these techniques cannot do, since that is the sharpest conclusion: the fixed-point statistic records the period of an associated recurrence and is blind to computational universality.

\section{Setup}

\begin{definition}
Let $\FF$ be the two-element field, written additively (so $1+1=0$). For $n \ge 1$ let $\mathbb{Z}/n$ index the lattice sites. A \emph{configuration} is a function $s : \mathbb{Z}/n \to \FF$; the set of configurations is $\Cfg(n)$, of cardinality $2^n$. A \emph{local rule} is a function $g : \FF^3 \to \FF$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{global update map} of $g$ is $F_g : \Cfg(n) \to \Cfg(n)$, $(F_g s)(i) = g(s(i-1), s(i), s(i+1))$, indices in $\mathbb{Z}/n$. A configuration $s$ is \emph{fixed} if $F_g s = s$; $V(g,n)$ is the set of fixed configurations and $\#V(g,n)$ its cardinality.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
For $r \in \mathbb{N}$ let $\mathrm{rule}(r)(a,b,c)$ be the $(4a+2b+c)$-th binary digit of $r$, and for a local rule $g$ set
$\nu(g) = \sum_{a,b,c} [\,g(a,b,c)=1\,]\,2^{4a+2b+c}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Decoding is a bijection]
$\mathrm{rule}(\nu(g)) = g$ for every local rule $g$, $\nu(\mathrm{rule}(r)) = r$ for every $r < 256$, and $\nu(g) < 256$ always. Hence $r \mapsto \mathrm{rule}(r)$ is a bijection from $\{0,\dots,255\}$ onto the set of local rules, which therefore has exactly $256$ elements.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
All three statements are finite identities of binary expansions, verified entry by entry over the $2^8$ rules and $2^3$ neighbourhoods.
\end{proof}

We use the standard algebraic normal forms
\[
g_{110} = b+c+bc+abc,\quad g_{150} = a+b+c,\quad g_{90} = a+c,\quad g_{30} = a+b+c+bc,
\]
\[
g_{51} = 1+b, \quad g_{170} = c, \quad g_{240} = a,
\]
each verified against its rule number by exhaustive comparison of truth tables.

\section{Shifts and equivariance}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{left} and \emph{right shifts} are $(\sigma^- s)(i) = s(i+1)$ and $(\sigma^+ s)(i) = s(i-1)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
$\sigma^-$ and $\sigma^+$ are mutually inverse $\FF$-linear automorphisms of $\Cfg(n)$, and $F_{\mathrm{rule}(170)} = \sigma^-$, $F_{\mathrm{rule}(240)} = \sigma^+$ identically.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Linearity is pointwise, and $(i+1)-1 = i$ in $\mathbb{Z}/n$. The identification follows from $g_{170}(a,b,c)=c$ and $g_{240}(a,b,c)=a$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Shift equivariance]\label{thm:equiv}
For every local rule $g$ and configuration $s$,
$F_g(\sigma^{\pm} s) = \sigma^{\pm}(F_g s)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Evaluating at $i$, the two sides are $g(s(i-1+1), s(i+1), s(i+1+1))$ and $g(s(i+1-1), s(i+1), s(i+1+1))$, equal since $i-1+1 = i = i+1-1$. The case of $\sigma^+$ follows by conjugation.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$V(g,n)$ is shift-stable, shifting preserves exact periods, $(\sigma^-)^k s = s(\cdot + k)$, and $F_g^{\,m}$ commutes with $\sigma^-$ for all $m$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{lemma}[Transitivity of translation]\label{lem:trans}
For $n \ge 1$ and $i,j \in \mathbb{Z}/n$ there is $k \in \mathbb{N}$ with $i + k = j$, namely the canonical representative of $j-i$ in $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$.
\end{lemma}

Lemma~\ref{lem:trans} converts a one-step local implication into a global statement; it is used in every propagation theorem below.

\section{The singleton criterion and its census}

\begin{definition}
A local rule $g$ is \emph{right-transitive at zero} if $g(a,0,c) = 0 \Rightarrow c = 0$ for all $a,c \in \FF$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Zero propagation]\label{lem:prop}
Let $g$ be right-transitive at zero, $s \in V(g,n)$ and $s(i) = 0$. Then $s(i+1) = 0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Fixedness at $i$ reads $g(s(i-1), s(i), s(i+1)) = s(i) = 0$; substituting $s(i)=0$ and applying right-transitivity gives $s(i+1)=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:exzero}
If $g(1,1,1) \ne 1$ and $n \ge 1$, every $s \in V(g,n)$ has a vanishing coordinate.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Otherwise $s \equiv 1$, and fixedness at $0$ gives $g(1,1,1) = 1$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Singleton Theorem]\label{thm:singleton}
Suppose $g$ is right-transitive at zero, $g(1,1,1) \ne 1$, and $g(0,0,0) = 0$. Then $V(g,n) = \{0\}$, hence $\#V(g,n)=1$, for every $n \ge 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $s$ be fixed and pick $i_0$ with $s(i_0)=0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:exzero}. Induction on $k$ using Lemma~\ref{lem:prop} gives $s(i_0+k)=0$ for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:trans} every site is of this form, so $s = 0$. Conversely $0$ is fixed since $g(0,0,0)=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Bit characterisation]\label{thm:bits}
A local rule satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:singleton} if and only if
$g(0,0,0)=0$, $g(0,0,1)=1$, $g(1,0,1)=1$, $g(1,1,1)=0$, i.e.\ bits $0,1,5,7$ of its rule number are $0,1,1,0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Right-transitivity is the conjunction of the two implications with $c=1$, i.e.\ $g(0,0,1)\ne 0$ and $g(1,0,1) \ne 0$; over $\FF$, ``$\ne 0$'' is ``$=1$''. The implications with $c=0$ are vacuous.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Census]\label{cor:census16}
Exactly $16$ of the $256$ rules satisfy the criterion, the four remaining bits being free, namely
\[
34,\ 38,\ 42,\ 46,\ 50,\ 54,\ 58,\ 62,\ 98,\ 102,\ 106,\ 110,\ 114,\ 118,\ 122,\ 126,
\]
and each has $\#V(g,n)=1$ for every $n \ge 1$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Rule 110]
$g_{110}(a,0,c) = c$, so Rule $110$ is right-transitive at zero; also $g_{110}(1,1,1) = 0$ and $g_{110}(0,0,0)=0$. Hence $V(110,n) = \{0\}$ and $\#V(110,n) = 1$ for every $n \ge 1$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}
Rule $46$ lies in the same census. Since by Theorem~\ref{thm:bits} the criterion depends on only four bits, Rules $46$ and $110$ agree in every bit relevant to the count, so $\#V(46,n)=\#V(110,n)=1$ for all $n$, although the standard qualitative taxonomy assigns them to different classes. No fixed-point statistic can separate them.
\end{remark}

\section{Symmetries as conjugacies}

\begin{definition}
Set $(\mir g)(a,b,c) = g(c,b,a)$ and $(\dual g)(a,b,c) = 1 + g(1+a,1+b,1+c)$; on configurations set $(\rho s)(i) = s(-i)$ and $(\kappa s)(i) = 1 + s(i)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Klein four-group]
$\mir$ and $\dual$ are commuting involutions on the set of local rules, and $\rho$, $\kappa$ are commuting involutions of $\Cfg(n)$, in particular injective. Thus $\{\mathrm{id}, \mir, \dual, \mir\circ\dual\}$ is a Klein four-group acting on the $256$ rules.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\mir\circ\mir = \mathrm{id}$ definitionally; for $\dual$ expand and use $1+(1+x)=x$, valid since $2=0$ in $\FF$. Commutation holds because reflection acts on positions and complementation on values.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Conjugacy]\label{thm:conj}
For every local rule $g$ and configuration $s$,
\[
F_{\mir g}(\rho s) = \rho(F_g s), \qquad F_{\dual g}(\kappa s) = \kappa(F_g s).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For the first, evaluate at $i$: the two sides are $g(s(-(i+1)), s(-i), s(-(i-1)))$ and $g(s(-i-1), s(-i), s(-i+1))$, equal since $-(i+1) = -i-1$ and $-(i-1) = -i+1$. For the second, expand $\dual$ and cancel double complements.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:conj} says the operations are genuine changes of coordinates, not merely relabellings of truth tables; every dynamical invariant transports.

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:classfn}
$\#V(\mir g, n) = \#V(\dual g, n) = \#V(g,n)$ for every $n$ and $g$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:conj}, $V(\mir g, n) = \rho(V(g,n))$ and $\rho$ is injective; likewise for $\kappa$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Injective semiconjugacy preserves exact periods]\label{lem:semiconj}
Let $f : A \to A$, $u : B \to B$ and let $e : A \to B$ be injective with $e \circ f = u \circ e$. Then $\per(u, e(x)) = \per(f,x)$ for every $x \in A$, both sides being $0$ when $x$ is not periodic.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction gives $e(f^k(x)) = u^k(e(x))$, so $u^k(e(x)) = e(x)$ iff $f^k(x) = x$ by injectivity. The two sets of periods coincide, so each minimal period divides the other.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$\per(F_{\mir g}, \rho s) = \per(F_g, s)$ and $\per(F_{\dual g}, \kappa s) = \per(F_g,s)$: the entire multiset of exact orbit lengths is a class function for the Klein four-group.
\end{corollary}

\begin{definition}
A rule $g$ satisfies the \emph{extended singleton criterion} if one of $g$, $\mir g$, $\dual g$, $\mir(\dual g)$ satisfies the criterion of Theorem~\ref{thm:singleton}.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Extended singleton theorem and census]\label{thm:ext}
If $g$ satisfies the extended criterion then $\#V(g,n)=1$ for every $n \ge 1$. Exactly $48$ of the $256$ rules satisfy it, three times the $16$ of Corollary~\ref{cor:census16}, which form a subset.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Combine Theorem~\ref{thm:singleton} with Corollary~\ref{cor:classfn} in each of the four cases; the census is a finite check over the $256$ rule numbers.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The partners of Rule 110]
$\mathrm{rule}(124) = \mir(g_{110})$, $\mathrm{rule}(137) = \dual(g_{110})$, $\mathrm{rule}(193) = \mir(\dual(g_{110}))$, whence
$\#V(124,n) = \#V(137,n) = \#V(193,n) = 1$ for every $n \ge 1$, although none of the three satisfies the local criterion. Rule $124$ additionally inherits the two-cycles of Theorem~\ref{thm:twocycle}: whenever $4 \mid n$ it has a configuration of exact period $2$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}
Since counting is a class function, classification statements about fixed points should be phrased on the $88$ symmetry classes rather than on rule numbers.
\end{remark}

\section{Periodic descent}

Fix $d \mid n$ and let $\pi : \mathbb{Z}/n \to \mathbb{Z}/d$ be the canonical ring homomorphism.

\begin{definition}
The \emph{pullback} $\pull : \Cfg(d) \to \Cfg(n)$ is $(\pull t)(i) = t(\pi(i))$; its image is exactly the set of $d$-periodic configurations.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Simulation embedding]\label{thm:pull}
For every rule $g$ and $d \mid n$, $\pull$ is injective and satisfies $F_g(\pull t) = \pull(F_g t)$. Hence $t \in V(g,d) \iff \pull t \in V(g,n)$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:semiconj}, $\per(F_g, \pull t) = \per(F_g, t)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\pi$ is a ring homomorphism, so $\pi(i\pm 1) = \pi(i) \pm 1$ and the local rule sees the same neighbourhood after pullback; injectivity follows from surjectivity of $\pi$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Divisibility monotonicity]
$\#V(g,d) \le \#V(g,n)$ whenever $d \mid n$, and every exact orbit length occurring at size $d$ occurs at size $n$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{lemma}[Descent]\label{lem:descent}
If $d \mid n$ and $s \in \Cfg(n)$ satisfies $s(i+d) = s(i)$ for all $i$, then $s = \pull t$ for some $t \in \Cfg(d)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Set $t(x) = s(\bar x)$ with $\bar x$ the canonical representative. Writing $\mathrm{val}(i) = (\mathrm{val}(i) \bmod d) + d\lfloor \mathrm{val}(i)/d\rfloor$ and iterating $d$-periodicity $\lfloor \mathrm{val}(i)/d \rfloor$ times gives $s(i) = t(\pi(i))$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Count invariance under descent]\label{thm:descount}
Let $d \mid n$ and suppose every $s \in V(g,n)$ is $d$-periodic. Then $\#V(g,n) = \#V(g,d)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:descent} and Theorem~\ref{thm:pull}, $V(g,n) = \pull(V(g,d))$; apply injectivity.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Coprime collapse]\label{lem:coprime}
If $\gcd(d,n)=1$, every $d$-periodic $s \in \Cfg(n)$ is constant.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
If $dv = 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}/n$, put $u = v(j-i)$ so that $du = j-i$; iterating $d$-periodicity $\mathrm{val}(u)$ times from $i$ gives $s(j) = s(i)$.
\end{proof}

For $d$ prime, Theorem~\ref{thm:descount} and Lemma~\ref{lem:coprime} together cover all $n$.

\section{Exact counting functions}

\subsection{Rule 150}

\begin{lemma}
$s \in V(150,n)$ if and only if $s(i-1) = s(i+1)$ for all $i$, i.e.\ $s$ is $2$-periodic. Every constant configuration is fixed.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The equation $s(i-1)+s(i)+s(i+1) = s(i)$ reduces to $s(i-1)=s(i+1)$; constants satisfy $c+c+c=c$ since $2c=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}
For every $n \ge 1$, $\#V(150,n) = 4$ if $n$ is even and $2$ if $n$ is odd.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For $n$ even, Theorem~\ref{thm:descount} with $d=2$ gives $\#V(150,n) = \#V(150,2) = 4$, all four length-$2$ configurations being fixed. For $n$ odd, $2$ is invertible mod $n$, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:coprime} every fixed configuration is constant; both constants are fixed and distinct.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Rule 90}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:90per}
Every $s \in V(90,n)$ satisfies $s(i+3) = s(i)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The fixed-point equation is the $\FF$ Fibonacci recurrence $s(i+1) = s(i) + s(i-1)$. Applying it at $i+1$ and $i+2$ and adding, the middle terms cancel since $2=0$, leaving $s(i+3)=s(i)$; equivalently, the Fibonacci recurrence over $\FF$ has period $3$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}
For every $n \ge 1$, $\#V(90,n) = 4$ if $3 \mid n$ and $1$ otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
If $3 \mid n$, Theorem~\ref{thm:descount} with $d = 3$ reduces to $\#V(90,3)=4$, a check over $8$ configurations. If $3 \nmid n$, Lemmas~\ref{lem:90per} and \ref{lem:coprime} force constancy, and the equation at a constant $c$ reads $c+c=c$, so $c=0$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Rule 30}

\begin{lemma}
$s \in V(30,n)$ if and only if $s(i-1) + s(i+1) + s(i)s(i+1) = 0$ for all $i$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:30per}
Every $s \in V(30,n)$ satisfies $s(i+2)=s(i)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The relation at $i+1$ reads $s(i) + s(i+2) + s(i+1)s(i+2) = 0$. If $s(i+1)=0$ this is $s(i)=s(i+2)$. If $s(i+1)=1$ it gives $s(i)=0$; the relation at $i+2$ then rules out $s(i+2)=1$, so $s(i+2)=0=s(i)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}
For every $n \ge 1$, $\#V(30,n) = 3$ if $n$ is even and $1$ if $n$ is odd.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For $n$ even descend to $d=2$: the fixed configurations of length $2$ are $00$, $01$, $10$. For $n$ odd, Lemmas~\ref{lem:30per} and \ref{lem:coprime} force constancy, and a constant $c$ satisfies $c+c+c^2=0$, i.e.\ $c^2 = 0$, so $c=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Rule $30$ is the standard chaotic exemplar, yet its count is as tame and as periodic in $n$ as those of the additive rules. The counts record the period of the recurrence cutting out the fixed set --- $2$, $3$, $2$ for rules $150$, $90$, $30$ --- an invariant of the linearisation of the rule, not of its dynamical complexity.
\end{remark}

\subsection{A count equal to two: the traffic rule}

\begin{lemma}[Leftward transitivity]\label{lem:left}
If $P$ is a property of sites with $P(i) \Rightarrow P(i-1)$ for all $i$, and $P(i_0)$ holds for some $i_0$, then $P$ holds at every site.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}
A local rule $g$ satisfies the \emph{constant-pair criterion} if
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{(zeros travel left)} $g(a,0,c)=0 \Rightarrow a = 0$;
\item \emph{(ones travel right)} $g(a,1,c)=1 \Rightarrow c = 1$;
\item $g(0,0,0)=0$ and $g(1,1,1)=1$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Constant-Pair Theorem]
If $g$ satisfies the constant-pair criterion then for every $n \ge 1$,
\[
V(g,n) = \{\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{1}\}, \qquad \#V(g,n) = 2,
\]
where $\mathbf 0$, $\mathbf 1$ are the two constant configurations.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $s$ be fixed. If $s(i)=0$ for some $i$, fixedness at $i$ gives $g(s(i-1),0,s(i+1)) = 0$, so $s(i-1)=0$ by condition~1; Lemma~\ref{lem:left} propagates this and $s = \mathbf 0$. Otherwise $s = \mathbf 1$. Conversely condition~3 makes both constants fixed, and they are distinct.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
Exactly four elementary rules satisfy the criterion, namely $176$, $178$, $184$, $186$. In particular the traffic rule $184$ has exactly two fixed configurations on every cyclic lattice, and so does its mirror image.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}
Condition~2 is not used in the proof of $V \subseteq \{\mathbf 0, \mathbf 1\}$; it is retained because it is the natural dual of condition~1 and the transparent statement of the traffic interpretation. Reading $1$ as an occupied cell and $0$ as empty road, with a car advancing exactly when the cell ahead is free, the theorem says that on a ring road the only stationary traffic states are the empty road and the complete jam, at every ring size.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}
Both propagation criteria are sufficient conditions only. Enumeration shows exactly $78$ rules have $\#V(g,n)=1$ for all $n \le 7$, of which only $48$ are certified for all $n$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:ext}; closing that gap is Conjecture~\ref{conj:finite}.
\end{remark}

\section{Orbits: what fixed points miss}

\begin{theorem}[Universal existence of periodic orbits]
For every rule $g$ and every $n \ge 1$ there are $s \in \Cfg(n)$ and $k>0$ with $F_g^{\,k}(s)=s$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The orbit $k \mapsto F_g^{\,k}(0)$ lies in a finite set, so $F_g^{\,a}(0) = F_g^{\,b}(0)$ for some $a<b$; then $F_g^{\,a}(0)$ has period $b-a>0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Rule 51]
Rule $51$, $g(a,b,c)=1+b$, is an involution of $\Cfg(n)$ with no fixed configuration: $\#V(51,n)=0$ for every $n \ge 1$, and every configuration has exact period $2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Rule 170: unbounded orbit lengths]
Let $\delta$ have $\delta(0)=1$ and $\delta(i)=0$ otherwise. Under Rule $170$ (the left shift), $\delta$ is $k$-periodic iff $n \mid k$; its exact period is $n$. Meanwhile $\#V(170,n)=2$ for every $n$, the fixed configurations being the two constants.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[An exact two-cycle of Rule 110]\label{thm:twocycle}
Let $t = 1110 \in \Cfg(4)$. Then $F_{110}^{\,2}(t) = t$ and $F_{110}(t) \ne t$, so $\per(F_{110}, t) = 2$. Consequently, by Theorem~\ref{thm:pull}, for every $n$ with $4 \mid n$ there is $s \in \Cfg(n)$ with $\per(F_{110},s) = 2$ and $s \ne 0$.
\end{theorem}

Explicitly, on $\Cfg(4)$ the configurations with $F_{110}^{\,2}(s)=s$ are $0000$, $1110$, $1011$, $1101$, $0111$: the fixed point together with two $2$-cycles $1110 \leftrightarrow 1011$ and $1101 \leftrightarrow 0111$. These are the smallest glider-like objects of Rule $110$, and their existence at every size divisible by $4$ is the content of Theorem~\ref{thm:twocycle}.

\begin{theorem}[Separation]
For every $n \ge 1$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\#V(90,n) \ne \#V(110,n)$ if and only if $3 \mid n$;
\item $\#V(110,n) < \#V(150,n)$ always;
\item $\#V(184,n) = 2 \ne 1 = \#V(110,n)$ always;
\item $\#V(46,n) = \#V(110,n)$ always, and likewise for the other fifteen rules of Corollary~\ref{cor:census16} and the partners $124$, $137$, $193$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

Items 1--3 show the statistic is not useless; item 4 shows precisely what it cannot do.

\section{The polynomial and scheme-theoretic model}\label{sec:poly}

\begin{definition}
For a local rule $g$ and $i \in \mathbb{Z}/n$ set
\[
P_{g,i} = \sum_{a,b,c \in \FF} g(a,b,c)\,(1+a+X_{i-1})(1+b+X_i)(1+c+X_{i+1}) \in \FF[X_j : j \in \mathbb{Z}/n],
\]
the factor $1+a+X_j$ being the $\FF$ indicator of the event $X_j = a$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Evaluation is the update map]\label{thm:eval}
$P_{g,i}(s) = (F_g s)(i)$ for every configuration $s$ and site $i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The claim reduces to the finite identity $\sum_{a,b,c} g(a,b,c)(1+a+x)(1+b+y)(1+c+z) = g(x,y,z)$ for $x,y,z \in \FF$, which holds since $1+a+x$ equals $1$ when $x=a$ and $0$ otherwise, so exactly one summand survives.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}
Renaming the variables by $X_j \mapsto X_{j+i}$ carries $P_{g,0}$ to $P_{g,i}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}
Let $I(g,n) = \big(\{P_{g,i}-X_i\}_i \cup \{X_i^2 - X_i\}_i\big)$, the second family being the Boolean relations forcing the coordinates to be bits.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Rational points]
A configuration $s$ annihilates every element of $I(g,n)$ if and only if $s \in V(g,n)$: the $\FF$-points of the fixed-point ideal are exactly the fixed configurations.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Forwards, apply the hypothesis to $P_{g,i}-X_i$ and use Theorem~\ref{thm:eval}. Backwards, every generator lies in the kernel of evaluation at $s$ --- the update generators by Theorem~\ref{thm:eval}, the Boolean generators because $c^2=c$ on $\FF$ --- and the kernel is an ideal.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$I(110,n) \ne (1)$ for every $n \ge 1$: the coordinate ring of the fixed-point scheme of Rule $110$ is nonzero, since $0$ is a rational point.
\end{corollary}

\section{Algorithms}

\paragraph{A. Transfer-matrix point count.}
The fixed configurations of $g$ on $\mathbb{Z}/n$ are exactly the closed walks of length $n$ in the \emph{fixed de Bruijn graph} $D(g)$: vertices are the four pairs $(a,b) \in \FF^2$, with an edge $(a,b) \to (b,c)$ precisely when $g(a,b,c)=b$. If $M(g)$ is its $4\times 4$ adjacency matrix then
\[
\#V(g,n) = \tr M(g)^n .
\]
This computes any single count in $O(\log n)$ multiplications of $4 \times 4$ matrices, against $\Theta(n2^n)$ for brute force, and it explains the phenomena above structurally: a constant count $1$ means the graph has a unique cycle; a count periodic with period $p$ means the spectrum consists of roots of unity of order dividing $p$ together with nilpotent directions.

\paragraph{B. Descent certification.}
To prove a formula for $\#V(g,\cdot)$ valid for all $n$: (1) find the least $d$ such that every fixed configuration is $d$-periodic; (2) compute $\#V(g,d)$ by enumerating $2^d$ configurations; (3) conclude $\#V(g,n) = \#V(g,d)$ for $d \mid n$; (4) solve the constant case for $n$ coprime to $d$. For prime $d$ the cases are exhaustive.

\paragraph{C. Symmetry-closed census.}
For each of the $256$ rule numbers, test the local criterion on the rule and its three symmetry partners, accepting if any passes. Each test inspects four truth-table entries, so the census costs $O(256\cdot 4\cdot 4)$ operations and certifies $48$ rules.

\section{Discussion}

There are three genuinely different reasons why $\#V(g,n)$ can be determined for all $n$ at once: a \emph{local} reason (a truth-table entry forces a bit to propagate, and cyclicity closes the argument); a \emph{conjugacy} reason (the rule is a change of coordinates away from one already understood); and an \emph{arithmetic} reason (the fixed-point equations form a recurrence of period $d$, and divisibility of $n$ by $d$ decides the count). Fifty-two of the $256$ rules are covered by the first two mechanisms alone; the third handles the additive rules $90$, $150$ and the nonlinear Rule $30$.

Against this the negative results are sharp. The count is a class function for a group of order four; it depends on Rule $110$ only through four bits of its table, shared with fifteen other rules including one of a different qualitative class; and it is constant in $n$ for the shift rule $170$, whose orbit lengths grow linearly. Any claimed correlation between fixed-point statistics and a qualitative classification must specify the boundary convention, the size range, the exact statistic, and the classification data --- and must survive the fact that no such statistic distinguishes Rule $46$ from Rule $110$ at any size.

The constructive alternative is the orbit spectrum: strictly finer, still a class function for the symmetry group, and transported along divisibility of lattice sizes by an injective simulation embedding. Since universality concerns unbounded space-time evolution, embeddings and orbit structures are the right invariants to pursue.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[Finite certification of the singleton property]\label{conj:finite}
For an elementary rule $g$ the following are equivalent: (i) $\#V(g,n)=1$ for every $n \ge 1$; (ii) $\#V(g,n)=1$ for $n=1,\dots,7$; (iii) the only bi-infinite $g$-fixed word is the all-zero word. Enumeration shows the set satisfying (ii) has exactly $78$ elements, of which $48$ are certified by the symmetry-closed criterion, so the conjecture predicts exactly $30$ further rules whose unit count needs a non-local argument.
\end{conjecture}

The key insight is that $\#V(g,n) = \tr M(g)^n$ for the $4\times 4$ fixed de Bruijn matrix, so a count that stays $1$ forever means that four-vertex graph has a unique cycle --- a decidable property. Hence a finite test must exist; the question is how small it can be.

Further programme:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Derive additional named singleton theorems as corollaries of the right-transitivity criterion, with periodic left and right shifts as explicit primitives.
\item Replace Boolean algebraic normal forms by polynomials over $\FF$ throughout and prove equality of polynomial evaluation with the global update map in that setting.
\item Specify the fixed-point coordinate ring using both the update equations and the Boolean relations $x_i^2-x_i$; study its Krull dimension separately from its number of $\FF$-rational points.
\item Formalise all $256$ rule tables from rule numbers and prove that rule-number decoding is a bijection with the set of local rules.
\item Compute fixed-point counts for every rule and bounded lattice size, then compare those finite invariants with a precisely encoded qualitative classification, stating the boundary convention, size range, statistic, and classification data explicitly.
\item Study periodic orbits of length greater than one; universality concerns unbounded space-time evolution, so orbit structure and simulation embeddings are more relevant invariants than fixed points alone.
\item Formulate any sheaf-theoretic construction explicitly: give the site, topology, restriction maps, and the intended theorem relating global sections to configurations, before comparing section structure across rules.
\end{enumerate}

by brute-force enumeration and, independently, by the 4x4 transfer-matrix formula

    #V(g, n) = trace( M(g)^n ),

where M(g) is the adjacency matrix of the "fixed de Bruijn graph" of the rule.

An elementary cellular automaton is a map g : F_2^3 -> F_2 (the local rule).
On the cyclic lattice Z/n it induces the global update

    (F_g s)(i) = g( s(i-1), s(i), s(i+1) ),      indices mod n.

A configuration s is FIXED when F_g s = s.  V(g, n) denotes the set of fixed
configurations, #V(g, n) its cardinality.

No third-party dependencies; pure Python 3, fully type-hinted.
Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from typing import Callable, Dict, Iterator, List, Sequence, Tuple

Bit = int
Neigh = Tuple[Bit, Bit, Bit]
Table = Dict[Neigh, Bit]
Config = Tuple[Bit, ...]
Matrix = List[List[int]]

NEIGHBOURHOODS: List[Neigh] = [(a, b, c) for a in (0, 1) for b in (0, 1) for c in (0, 1)]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Rules, rule numbers, and the global update map
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def rule_table(number: int) -> Table:
    """Decode a Wolfram rule number: the output on (a, b, c) is bit 4a+2b+c."""
    return {(a, b, c): (number >> (4 * a + 2 * b + c)) & 1 for (a, b, c) in NEIGHBOURHOODS}


def rule_number(table: Table) -> int:
    """Encode a local rule as its Wolfram rule number (inverse of `rule_table`)."""
    return sum(2 ** (4 * a + 2 * b + c) for (a, b, c) in NEIGHBOURHOODS if table[(a, b, c)] == 1)


def step(table: Table, s: Config) -> Config:
    """One synchronous update of the whole cyclic lattice."""
    n = len(s)
    return tuple(table[(s[(i - 1) % n], s[i], s[(i + 1) % n])] for i in range(n))


def configs(n: int) -> Iterator[Config]:
    """All 2^n configurations on the cyclic lattice of n sites."""
    return product((0, 1), repeat=n)


def fixed_configs(number: int, n: int) -> List[Config]:
    """V(g, n): all fixed configurations, by brute-force enumeration."""
    t = rule_table(number)
    return [s for s in configs(n) if step(t, s) == s]


def fixed_count(number: int, n: int) -> int:
    """#V(g, n), by brute-force enumeration.  Cost Theta(n * 2^n)."""
    return len(fixed_configs(number, n))


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  The transfer matrix: #V(g, n) = trace M(g)^n
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def fixed_de_bruijn_matrix(number: int) -> Matrix:
    """
    Adjacency matrix of the de Bruijn graph on overlapping pairs (a, b),
    restricted to the edges (a, b) -> (b, c) with g(a, b, c) = b.

    Fixed configurations of length n are exactly the closed walks of length n.
    """
    t = rule_table(number)
    m: Matrix = [[0] * 4 for _ in range(4)]
    for (a, b, c) in NEIGHBOURHOODS:
        if t[(a, b, c)] == b:
            m[2 * a + b][2 * b + c] += 1
    return m


def mat_mul(a: Matrix, b: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    k = len(a)
    return [[sum(a[i][t] * b[t][j] for t in range(k)) for j in range(k)] for i in range(k)]


def mat_pow(a: Matrix, n: int) -> Matrix:
    """Fast exponentiation: O(log n) multiplications of 4x4 matrices."""
    k = len(a)
    result: Matrix = [[1 if i == j else 0 for j in range(k)] for i in range(k)]
    base = [row[:] for row in a]
    e = n
    while e > 0:
        if e & 1:
            result = mat_mul(result, base)
        base = mat_mul(base, base)
        e >>= 1
    return result


def fixed_count_fast(number: int, n: int) -> int:
    """#V(g, n) in O(log n) 4x4 matrix products, valid for arbitrarily large n."""
    p = mat_pow(fixed_de_bruijn_matrix(number), n)
    return sum(p[i][i] for i in range(4))


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  The two propagation criteria
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def right_transitive(t: Table) -> bool:
    """g(a, 0, c) = 0  ==>  c = 0 :  zeros propagate rightwards."""
    return all(t[(a, 0, c)] != 0 or c == 0 for a in (0, 1) for c in (0, 1))


def singleton_criterion(t: Table) -> bool:
    """Right-transitive, kills the all-ones pattern, fixes the all-zero pattern."""
    return right_transitive(t) and t[(1, 1, 1)] != 1 and t[(0, 0, 0)] == 0


def constant_pair_criterion(t: Table) -> bool:
    """Zeros travel left, ones travel right, and both constants are fixed."""
    left_zero = all(t[(a, 0, c)] != 0 or a == 0 for a in (0, 1) for c in (0, 1))
    right_one = all(t[(a, 1, c)] != 1 or c == 1 for a in (0, 1) for c in (0, 1))
    return left_zero and right_one and t[(0, 0, 0)] == 0 and t[(1, 1, 1)] == 1


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  The Klein four-group of symmetries
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def mirror(t: Table) -> Table:
    """Reflection: read the neighbourhood right-to-left."""
    return {(a, b, c): t[(c, b, a)] for (a, b, c) in NEIGHBOURHOODS}


def dual(t: Table) -> Table:
    """Complementation: swap the two letters of F_2 on inputs and outputs."""
    return {(a, b, c): 1 ^ t[(1 ^ a, 1 ^ b, 1 ^ c)] for (a, b, c) in NEIGHBOURHOODS}


def klein_orbit(number: int) -> List[int]:
    t = rule_table(number)
    return sorted({rule_number(f(t)) for f in
                   (lambda x: x, mirror, dual, lambda x: mirror(dual(x)))})


def ext_singleton_criterion(t: Table) -> bool:
    """The rule, or one of its three symmetry partners, passes the local criterion."""
    return any(singleton_criterion(f(t)) for f in
               (lambda x: x, mirror, dual, lambda x: mirror(dual(x))))


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Orbits
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def exact_period(number: int, s: Config) -> int:
    """Minimal k > 0 with F_g^k(s) = s, or 0 if s is not on a periodic orbit."""
    t = rule_table(number)
    seen: Dict[Config, int] = {s: 0}
    cur = s
    for k in range(1, 2 ** len(s) + 2):
        cur = step(t, cur)
        if cur == s:
            return k
        if cur in seen:
            return 0
        seen[cur] = k
    return 0


def pull(t_small: Config, n: int) -> Config:
    """Periodic descent: pull a configuration on Z/d back to Z/n, for d | n."""
    d = len(t_small)
    if n % d != 0:
        raise ValueError(f"{d} does not divide {n}")
    return tuple(t_small[i % d] for i in range(n))


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Reporting helpers
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def banner(title: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 74)


def check(claim: str, ok: bool) -> None:
    print(f"  [{'OK ' if ok else 'FAIL'}]  {claim}")
    assert ok, claim

def demo_singleton_theorem(max_n: int = 14) -> None:
    banner("1.  The Rule 110 Singleton Theorem:  #V(110, n) = 1 for every n")
    print("  Rule 110 has g(a,0,c) = c, so a zero forces its right neighbour to zero;")
    print("  the all-ones configuration is destroyed since g(1,1,1) = 0.  Cyclicity")
    print("  then sweeps the lattice, leaving only the all-zero configuration.\n")
    counts = [fixed_count(110, n) for n in range(1, max_n + 1)]
    print(f"  #V(110, n) for n = 1..{max_n}:  {counts}")
    check("count is identically 1 up to n = %d" % max_n, all(c == 1 for c in counts))
    check("the transfer matrix agrees for n up to 10**6",
          all(fixed_count_fast(110, n) == 1 for n in (10, 1000, 10 ** 6)))
    print("\n  Census of the local criterion (four bits of the rule number are pinned):")
    cert = [r for r in range(256) if singleton_criterion(rule_table(r))]
    print(f"    {len(cert)} rules: {cert}")
    check("exactly 16 rules pass the local singleton criterion", len(cert) == 16)
    check("Rule 110 is among them", 110 in cert)
    check("Rule 46 is among them (same four critical bits as Rule 110)", 46 in cert)
    check("every certified rule has #V = 1 up to n = 12",
          all(fixed_count(r, n) == 1 for r in cert for n in range(1, 13)))


def demo_symmetry_census() -> None:
    banner("2.  Reflection and complementation: a Klein four-group of conjugacies")
    print("  Reflecting the lattice conjugates the dynamics of g to that of mirror(g);")
    print("  complementing all cells conjugates it to that of dual(g).  Both the")
    print("  fixed-point count and every exact orbit period are therefore invariant.\n")
    print(f"  Klein orbit of Rule 110: {klein_orbit(110)}")
    check("the partners of Rule 110 are 110, 124, 137, 193",
          klein_orbit(110) == [110, 124, 137, 193])
    for r in (124, 137, 193):
        counts = [fixed_count(r, n) for n in range(1, 13)]
        local = singleton_criterion(rule_table(r))
        print(f"    Rule {r:3d}: #V = {counts[0]} for all tested n"
              f" (passes the LOCAL criterion: {local})")
        check(f"#V({r}, n) = 1 for n <= 12", all(c == 1 for c in counts))
    ext = [r for r in range(256) if ext_singleton_criterion(rule_table(r))]
    loc = [r for r in range(256) if singleton_criterion(rule_table(r))]
    print(f"\n  Local census: {len(loc)} rules.  Symmetry-closed census: {len(ext)} rules.")
    check("the symmetry-closed census has exactly 48 rules", len(ext) == 48)
    check("it contains the local census", set(loc) <= set(ext))
    check("every certified rule really has #V = 1 up to n = 12",
          all(fixed_count(r, n) == 1 for r in ext for n in range(1, 13)))


def demo_arithmetic_counts(max_n: int = 14) -> None:
    banner("3.  Counts that are arithmetic functions of the lattice size")

    def predicted_150(n: int) -> int:
        return 4 if n % 2 == 0 else 2

    def predicted_90(n: int) -> int:
        return 4 if n % 3 == 0 else 1

    def predicted_30(n: int) -> int:
        return 3 if n % 2 == 0 else 1

    for number, predict, formula in (
        (150, predicted_150, "4 if n even, 2 if n odd      (2-periodic fixed configs)"),
        (90, predicted_90, "4 if 3 | n, 1 otherwise      (F_2 Fibonacci, period 3)"),
        (30, predicted_30, "3 if n even, 1 if n odd      (nonlinear, still 2-periodic)"),
    ):
        counts = [fixed_count(number, n) for n in range(1, max_n + 1)]
        print(f"\n  Rule {number}:  {formula}")
        print(f"    enumerated : {counts}")
        print(f"    predicted  : {[predict(n) for n in range(1, max_n + 1)]}")
        check(f"formula for rule {number} holds up to n = {max_n}",
              all(fixed_count(number, n) == predict(n) for n in range(1, max_n + 1)))
        check(f"transfer matrix reproduces rule {number} for huge n",
              all(fixed_count_fast(number, n) == predict(n)
                  for n in (30, 31, 999, 1000, 10 ** 5, 10 ** 5 + 1)))


def demo_traffic_rule(max_n: int = 14) -> None:
    banner("4.  The traffic rule 184: exactly two fixed configurations, always")
    print("  Reading 1 as 'car' and 0 as 'empty road', Rule 184 advances a car exactly")
    print("  when the cell ahead is free.  Its table satisfies: g(a,0,c)=0 forces a=0")
    print("  (emptiness travels LEFT) and g(a,1,c)=1 forces c=1 (cars travel RIGHT).")
    print("  Hence the only stationary states are the empty road and the total jam.\n")
    counts = [fixed_count(184, n) for n in range(1, max_n + 1)]
    print(f"  #V(184, n) for n = 1..{max_n}:  {counts}")
    check("count is identically 2", all(c == 2 for c in counts))
    check("the two fixed configurations are the constants",
          all(set(fixed_configs(184, n)) == {(0,) * n, (1,) * n} for n in range(1, 11)))
    cp = [r for r in range(256) if constant_pair_criterion(rule_table(r))]
    print(f"\n  Census of the constant-pair criterion: {len(cp)} rules: {cp}")
    check("exactly the four rules 176, 178, 184, 186", cp == [176, 178, 184, 186])
    check("all four have #V = 2 up to n = 12",
          all(fixed_count(r, n) == 2 for r in cp for n in range(1, 13)))
    print("\n  A jam relaxing on a ring of 16 sites (Rule 184, 8 time steps):")
    t = rule_table(184)
    s: Config = tuple(1 if i in (3, 4, 5, 6, 10) else 0 for i in range(16))
    for _ in range(8):
        print("    " + "".join("#" if b else "." for b in s))
        s = step(t, s)


def demo_orbits() -> None:
    banner("5.  Orbits: what the fixed-point count cannot see")
    print("  Rule 51 (complement every cell) has NO fixed configuration at all,")
    print("  yet every configuration lies on an orbit of exact period two.")
    for n in range(1, 9):
        periods = {exact_period(51, s) for s in configs(n)}
        check(f"n = {n}: #V(51,n) = 0 and every exact period is 2",
              fixed_count(51, n) == 0 and periods == {2})

    print("\n  Rule 170 (the left shift) has #V = 2 for every n (the two constants),")
    print("  yet the one-hot configuration has exact period exactly n:")
    for n in range(1, 11):
        delta: Config = tuple(1 if i == 0 else 0 for i in range(n))
        p = exact_period(170, delta)
        check(f"n = {n:2d}: #V(170,n) = 2 and per(delta) = {p}",
              fixed_count(170, n) == 2 and p == n)

    print("\n  Rule 110 has a genuine two-cycle on the four-site lattice.")
    t110: Config = (1, 1, 1, 0)
    tbl = rule_table(110)
    print(f"    1110 -> {''.join(map(str, step(tbl, t110)))}"
          f" -> {''.join(map(str, step(tbl, step(tbl, t110))))}")
    check("1110 has exact period 2 on Z/4", exact_period(110, t110) == 2)
    two_per = [s for s in configs(4) if step(tbl, step(tbl, s)) == s]
    print("    All 2-periodic configurations on Z/4: "
          + ", ".join("".join(map(str, s)) for s in two_per))
    check("they are the fixed point plus two 2-cycles", len(two_per) == 5)
    print("\n  Periodic descent transports the two-cycle to every n divisible by 4:")
    for n in (4, 8, 12, 16):
        s = pull(t110, n)
        p = exact_period(110, s)
        check(f"n = {n:2d}: pull(1110) has exact period {p}, and #V(110,n) = 1",
              p == 2 and fixed_count(110, min(n, 14)) == 1)


def demo_separation() -> None:
    banner("6.  Which rules the fixed-point statistic separates - and which it does not")
    print("  (a) #V(90,n) differs from #V(110,n) exactly on the multiples of 3:")
    for n in range(1, 13):
        d = fixed_count(90, n) != fixed_count(110, n)
        check(f"n = {n:2d}: differ = {d}, 3 | n = {n % 3 == 0}", d == (n % 3 == 0))
    print("\n  (b) #V(110,n) < #V(150,n) for every n:")
    check("strict inequality up to n = 14",
          all(fixed_count(110, n) < fixed_count(150, n) for n in range(1, 15)))
    print("\n  (c) but #V(46,n) = #V(110,n) for every n, although the two rules are")
    print("      placed in different qualitative classes: the statistic is blind here.")
    check("rules 46 and 110 agree up to n = 14",
          all(fixed_count(46, n) == fixed_count(110, n) for n in range(1, 15)))
    same_bits = all(rule_table(46)[k] == rule_table(110)[k]
                    for k in ((0, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1), (1, 0, 1), (1, 1, 1)))
    check("they agree in exactly the four bits governing the count", same_bits)


def demo_transfer_matrix() -> None:
    banner("7.  The transfer matrix, and how far the enumeration can be trusted")
    print("  #V(g, n) = trace M(g)^n, where M(g) is the 4x4 adjacency matrix of the")
    print("  de Bruijn graph on pairs (a,b) with edges (a,b) -> (b,c) when g(a,b,c) = b.\n")
    for r in (110, 90, 150, 30, 184, 51):
        m = fixed_de_bruijn_matrix(r)
        brute = [fixed_count(r, n) for n in range(1, 13)]
        fast = [fixed_count_fast(r, n) for n in range(1, 13)]
        print(f"  Rule {r:3d}: M = {m}")
        print(f"            trace M^n = {fast}")
        check(f"transfer matrix matches enumeration for rule {r}", brute == fast)
    print("\n  Full agreement over all 256 rules and all n <= 12:")
    ok = all(fixed_count(r, n) == fixed_count_fast(r, n)
             for r in range(256) for n in range(1, 13))
    check("all 256 rules, n = 1..12", ok)
    print("\n  Rules whose count is 1 for every n <= 7 (candidates for the singleton")
    print("  property), compared with the 48 certified by symmetry-closed propagation:")
    unit = [r for r in range(256) if all(fixed_count_fast(r, n) == 1 for n in range(1, 8))]
    ext = [r for r in range(256) if ext_singleton_criterion(rule_table(r))]
    print(f"    candidates: {len(unit)}   certified: {len(ext)}   gap: {len(unit) - len(ext)}")
    check("78 candidates, 48 certified, 30 open", (len(unit), len(ext)) == (78, 48))
    check("certified rules are candidates", set(ext) <= set(unit))
    check("all 78 candidates still have count 1 at n = 40 (evidence for the conjecture)",
          all(fixed_count_fast(r, 40) == 1 for r in unit))


def main() -> None:
    print(__doc__)
    demo_singleton_theorem()
    demo_symmetry_census()
    demo_arithmetic_counts()
    demo_traffic_rule()
    demo_orbits()
    demo_separation()
    demo_transfer_matrix()
    banner("All checks passed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

    left_zero = all(t[(a, 0, c)] != 0 or a == 0 for a in (0, 1) for c in (0, 1))
    right_one = all(t[(a, 1, c)] != 1 or c == 1 for a in (0, 1) for c in (0, 1))
    return left_zero and right_one and t[(0, 0, 0)] == 0 and t[(1, 1, 1)] == 1


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  The Klein four-group of symmetries
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def mirror(t: Table) -> Table:
    """Reflection: read the neighbourhood right-to-left."""
    return {(a, b, c): t[(c, b, a)] for (a, b, c) in NEIGHBOURHOODS}


def dual(t: Table) -> Table:
    """Complementation: swap the two letters of F_2 on inputs and outputs."""
    return {(a, b, c): 1 ^ t[(1 ^ a, 1 ^ b, 1 ^ c)] for (a, b, c) in NEIGHBOURHOODS}


def klein_orbit(number: int) -> List[int]:
    t = rule_table(number)
    return sorted({rule_number(f(t)) for f in
                   (lambda x: x, mirror, dual, lambda x: mirror(dual(x)))})


def ext_singleton_criterion(t: Table) -> bool:
    """The rule, or one of its three symmetry partners, passes the local criterion."""
    return any(singleton_criterion(f(t)) for f in
               (lambda x: x, mirror, dual, lambda x: mirror(dual(x))))


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Orbits
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def exact_period(number: int, s: Config) -> int:
    """Minimal k > 0 with F_g^k(s) = s, or 0 if s is not on a periodic orbit."""
    t = rule_table(number)
    seen: Dict[Config, int] = {s: 0}
    cur = s
    for k in range(1, 2 ** len(s) + 2):
        cur = step(t, cur)
        if cur == s:
            return k
        if cur in seen:
            return 0
        seen[cur] = k
    return 0


def pull(t_small: Config, n: int) -> Config:
    """Periodic descent: pull a configuration on Z/d back to Z/n, for d | n."""
    d = len(t_small)
    if n % d != 0:
        raise ValueError(f"{d} does not divide {n}")
    return tuple(t_small[i % d] for i in range(n))

def demo_singleton_theorem(max_n: int = 14) -> None:

    print("  then sweeps the lattice, leaving only the all-zero configuration.\n")
    counts = [fixed_count(110, n) for n in range(1, max_n + 1)]

def demo_orbits() -> None:
    banner("5.  Orbits: what the fixed-point count cannot see")
    print("  Rule 51 (complement every cell) has NO fixed configuration at all,")
    print("  yet every configuration lies on an orbit of exact period two.")
    for n in range(1, 9):
        periods = {exact_period(51, s) for s in configs(n)}
        check(f"n = {n}: #V(51,n) = 0 and every exact period is 2",
              fixed_count(51, n) == 0 and periods == {2})

    print("\n  Rule 170 (the left shift) has #V = 2 for every n (the two constants),")
    print("  yet the one-hot configuration has exact period exactly n:")
    for n in range(1, 11):
        delta: Config = tuple(1 if i == 0 else 0 for i in range(n))
        p = exact_period(170, delta)
        check(f"n = {n:2d}: #V(170,n) = 2 and per(delta) = {p}",
              fixed_count(170, n) == 2 and p == n)

    print("\n  Rule 110 has a genuine two-cycle on the four-site lattice.")
    t110: Config = (1, 1, 1, 0)
    tbl = rule_table(110)
    print(f"    1110 -> {''.join(map(str, step(tbl, t110)))}"
          f" -> {''.join(map(str, step(tbl, step(tbl, t110))))}")
    check("1110 has exact period 2 on Z/4", exact_period(110, t110) == 2)
    two_per = [s for s in configs(4) if step(tbl, step(tbl, s)) == s]
    print("    All 2-periodic configurations on Z/4: "
          + ", ".join("".join(map(str, s)) for s in two_per))
    check("they are the fixed point plus two 2-cycles", len(two_per) == 5)
    print("\n  Periodic descent transports the two-cycle to every n divisible by 4:")
    for n in (4, 8, 12, 16):
        s = pull(t110, n)
        p = exact_period(110, s)
        check(f"n = {n:2d}: pull(1110) has exact period {p}, and #V(110,n) = 1",
              p == 2 and fixed_count(110, min(n, 14)) == 1)


def demo_separation() -> None:
    banner("6.  Which rules the fixed-point statistic separates - and which it does not")
    print("  (a) #V(90,n) differs from #V(110,n) exactly on the multiples of 3:")
    for n in range(1, 13):
        d = fixed_count(90, n) != fixed_count(110, n)
        check(f"n = {n:2d}: differ = {d}, 3 | n = {n % 3 == 0}", d == (n % 3 == 0))
    print("\n  (b) #V(110,n) < #V(150,n) for every n:")

NEIGHBOURHOODS: List[Neigh] = [(a, b, c) for a in (0, 1) for b in (0, 1) for c in (0, 1)]


def rule_table(number: int) -> Table:
    return {(a, b, c): (number >> (4 * a + 2 * b + c)) & 1 for (a, b, c) in NEIGHBOURHOODS}


def step(t: Table, s: Config) -> Config:
    n = len(s)
    return tuple(t[(s[(i - 1) % n], s[i], s[(i + 1) % n])] for i in range(n))


def pull(t_small: Config, n: int) -> Config:
    """Repeat a configuration of length d around a ring of length n, for d | n."""
    d = len(t_small)
    if n % d:
        raise ValueError(f"{d} does not divide {n}")
    return tuple(t_small[i % d] for i in range(n))


def fixed_configs(number: int, n: int) -> List[Config]:
    t = rule_table(number)
    return [s for s in product((0, 1), repeat=n) if step(t, s) == s]


def exact_period(number: int, s: Config) -> int:
    """Least k > 0 with F^k(s) = s, or 0 if s is not periodic."""
    t = rule_table(number)
    cur, seen = s, {s}
    for k in range(1, 2 ** len(s) + 2):
        cur = step(t, cur)
        if cur == s:
            return k
        if cur in seen:
            return 0
        seen.add(cur)
    return 0

            small = list(product((0, 1), repeat=d))
            intertwines = all(step(t, pull(u, n)) == pull(step(t, u), n) for u in small)
            injective = len({pull(u, n) for u in small}) == len(small)
            periods = all(exact_period(number, pull(u, n)) == exact_period(number, u)
                          for u in small)
            check(f"rule {number:3d}, {d} | {n}: intertwines={intertwines}, "

def rule_table(number: int) -> Table:

    return {(a, b, c): (number >> (4 * a + 2 * b + c)) & 1 for (a, b, c) in NEIGHBOURHOODS}


def fixed_de_bruijn_matrix(number: int) -> Matrix:
    """Adjacency matrix of D(g), on the vertex order (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)."""
    t = rule_table(number)
    m: Matrix = [[0] * 4 for _ in range(4)]
    for (a, b, c) in NEIGHBOURHOODS:
        if t[(a, b, c)] == b:
            m[2 * a + b][2 * b + c] += 1
    return m


def mat_mul(a: Matrix, b: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    k = len(a)
    return [[sum(a[i][t] * b[t][j] for t in range(k)) for j in range(k)] for i in range(k)]


def mat_pow(a: Matrix, n: int) -> Matrix:
    """Binary exponentiation; exact integer arithmetic, so valid for astronomically large n."""
    k = len(a)
    result: Matrix = [[1 if i == j else 0 for j in range(k)] for i in range(k)]
    base = [row[:] for row in a]
    while n > 0:
        if n & 1:
            result = mat_mul(result, base)
        base = mat_mul(base, base)
        n >>= 1
    return result

    """#V(g, n), the number of configurations on Z/n fixed by the rule."""
    p = mat_pow(fixed_de_bruijn_matrix(number), n)
    return sum(p[i][i] for i in range(4))

def draw(ax, number: int, caption: str) -> None:
    pos = [(cos(pi / 2 + k * pi / 2), sin(pi / 2 + k * pi / 2)) for k in range(4)]
    ax.set_xlim(-1.7, 1.7)
    ax.set_ylim(-1.7, 1.7)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axis("off")
    for (u, v) in edges(number):

            ax.add_patch(Circle((x * 1.28, y * 1.28), 0.19, fill=False,

                                         shrinkA=17, shrinkB=17))
    for k, (x, y) in enumerate(pos):
        ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), 0.17, facecolor="white", edgecolor="0.2", lw=1.4, zorder=3))
        ax.text(x, y, VERTEX_LABELS[k], ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10, zorder=4)
    ax.set_title(caption, fontsize=10)


def main() -> None:
    panels = [
        (110, "rule 110:  one cycle  →  #V = 1 for all n"),
        (184, "rule 184:  two loops  →  #V = 2 for all n"),
        (90, "rule 90:  loop + 3-cycle  →  #V = 4 iff 3 | n"),
        (150, "rule 150:  two loops + 2-cycle  →  #V = 4 iff 2 | n"),
        (30, "rule 30:  loop + 2-cycle  →  #V = 3 iff 2 | n"),

    for ax, (r, cap) in zip(axes.ravel(), panels):

    fig.suptitle("Fixed de Bruijn graphs:  vertices are cell pairs (a,b), "
                 "edges (a,b)→(b,c) are the neighbourhoods with g(a,b,c) = b", fontsize=12)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("de_bruijn_graphs.png", dpi=150)
    print("wrote de_bruijn_graphs.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

<div class="wrap">
